Simpler Optimal Sorting from a Directed Acyclic Graph

**Abstract**

Fredman proposed in 1976 the following algorithmic problem: Given are a ground set _X_, some partial order _P_ over _X_, and some comparison oracle _O<sub>L</sub>_ that specifies a linear order _L_ over _X_ that extends _P_. A _query_ to _O<sub>L</sub>_ has as input distinct \(x,x'\in X\) and outputs whether \(x<Lx'\) or vice versa. If we denote by _e(P_) the number of linear orders that extend _P_, then it follows from basic information theory that log_e(P_) is a worst-case lower bound on the number of queries needed to output the sorted order of _X_.

Fredman did not specify in what form the partial order is given. Haeupler, Hladík, Iacono, Rozhon, Tarjan, and Tˇtek (’24) propose to assume as input a directed acyclic graph, _G_, with _m_ edges and _n_=|_X_| vertices. Denote by _P<sub>G</sub>_ the partial order induced by _G_. Their algorithmic performance is measured in running time and the number of queries used, where they use \(\Theta(m+n+loge(P_G))\) time and \(\Theta(loge(P_G))\) queries to output _X_ in its sorted order. Their algorithm is worst-case optimal in terms of running time and queries, both. Their algorithm combines topological sorting with heapsort. Their analysis relies upon sophisticated counting arguments using entropy, recursively defined sets defined over the run of their algorithm, and vertices in the graph that they identify as bottlenecks for sorting.

In this paper, we do away with sophistication. We show that when the input is a directed acyclic graph then the problem admits a simple solution using \(\Theta(m+n+loge(P_G))\) time and \(\Theta(loge(P_G))\) queries. Especially our proofs are much simpler as we avoid the usage of advanced charging arguments and data structures, and instead rely upon two brief observations.

## 1 Introduction

Sorting is a fundamental problem in computer science. In 1976, Fredman introduced a natural generalisation of sorting, namely sorting under partial information [4]:

Given a ground set _X_ of size _n_, and some partial order _P_ on _X_, and an oracle _O<sub>L</sub>_ with access to a ground-truth linear order _L_ of _X_, the task is to minimise the number of oracle queries to recover the linear order of _X_. A query takes two input elements from _X_, and outputs their relation in the linear order. Algorithmic efficiency is measured in time, and the number of queries used. Let _e(P_) denote the number of linear orders that extend the partial order _P_. Then, for any binary (e.g. yes/no) query, \(\lceil log_2(e(P))\rceil\) is a worst-case lower bound for the number of queries needed, simply because the sequence of answers should be able to lead to any possible extension of the order.

Ivor van der Hoog, Eva Rotenberg, Daniel Rutschmann. Technical University of Denmark, DTU

arXiv:2407.21591v6 [cs.DS] 7 Feb 2026

## Previous work.

Fredman \[4, TCS’76\] shows an exponential-time algorithm for sorting under partial information that uses log_e(P_)+_O(n_) queries. This fails to match the \(\Omega(loge(P))\) lower bound when log_e(P_) is sublinear. Kahn and Saks \[9, Order’84\] prove that there always exists a query which reduces the number of remaining linear extensions by a constant fraction; showing that an _O_(log_e(P_))-query algorithm exists. Kahn and Kim \[8, S’92\] are the first to also consider algorithmic running time. They note that Kahn and Saks \[9\] can preprocess a partial order using exponential time and space, so that given _O<sub>L</sub>_ it can output the sorted order of _X_ in linear time plus _O_(log_e(P_)) queries. Kahn and Kim \[8, S’92\] propose the first polynomial-time algorithm that performs _O_(log_e(P_)) queries. They do not separate preprocessing the partial order and oracle queries, and use an unspecified polynomial time using the ellipsoid method. Cardinal, Fiorini, Joret, Jungers and Munro \[3, S’10\] (in their full version in Combinatorica) preprocess _P_ in _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time, to output the sorted _X_ in _O_(log_e(P_)+_n_) time using _O_(log_e(P_)) queries. Their runtime poses the question whether query-optimal (sub)quadratic-time algorithms are possible.

For subquadratic algorithms, it becomes relevant how one obtains the partial order. Van der Hoog, Kostityna, Löffler and Speckmann \[11, SOCG’19\] study the problem in a restricted setting where _P_ is induced by a set of intervals. Here, distinct \(x_i,x_j\in X\) are incomparable whenever their intervals (\[_a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>_\],\[_a<sub>j</sub>,b<sub>j</sub>_\]) intersect (otherwise, \(x_i\prec_Px_j\) whenever _b<sub>i</sub>\<a<sub>j</sub>_). They preprocess the intervals in _O(n_log_n_) time such that, given _O<sub>L</sub>_, they can produce a pointer to a linked list storing _X_ in its sorted order using _O_(log_e(P_)) queries and time. For their queries, they use _finger search_ \[2\] (i.e., _exponential search_ from a pointer). Finger search has as input a value _x<sub>i</sub>_, a sorted list \(\pi\), and a finger \(p\in\pi\) with _p\<x<sub>i</sub>_. It finds the farthest _q_ along \(\pi\) for which _q\<x<sub>i</sub>_ in _O_(1+log_d<sub>i</sub>_) time and comparisons. Here, _d<sub>i</sub>_ denotes the length of the sublist from _p_ to _q_ \[2\].

Van der Hoog and Rutschmann \[7, FOCS’24\] assume that _P_ is given as another oracle _O<sub>P</sub>_ where queries receive distinct \(x,x'\in X\) and output whether \(x\prec_Px'\). For fixed \(c\ge 1\), they preprocess _O<sub>P</sub>_ using \(O(n^{1+\frac{1}{c}})\) time and queries to _O<sub>P</sub>_. Given _O<sub>L</sub>_, they produce a pointer to a linked list storing _X_ in its sorted order using \(O(c\cdot loge(P))\) queries and time. Their query algorithm also makes use of finger search. They show matching lower bounds in their setting.

Haeupler, Hladík, Iacono, Rozhon, Tarjan, and Tˇtek \[5, ’24\] assume that the partial order _P<sub>G</sub>_ is induced by a graph _G_ with _m_ edges. Their algorithm can be seen as a combination of topological sort and heapsort. Their algorithm first isolates a collection \(B\subset X\) which they call _bottlenecks_. They then iteratively consider all sources _S_ in _G-B_, remove the source \(s\in S\) that is _minimum_ in the linear order _L_, and append _s_ to the output \(\pi\). Before appending _s_ to \(\pi\), they find the maximum prefix \(B_s=\{b\in B|b<_Ls\}\) using finger search where the finger is the head of _B_. They remove _B<sub>s</sub>_ from _B_, append _B<sub>s</sub>_ to \(\pi\), and then append _s_. To obtain the minimum \(s\in S\), they store all current sources of the graph in a _heap_ where comparisons in the heap use the linear oracle _O<sub>L</sub>_. Their algorithm does not separate preprocessing the graph _G_, and oracle queries. It uses \(\Theta(n+m+loge(P_G))\) overall time and \(\Theta(loge(P))\) linear oracle queries. Since reading the input takes at least \(\Omega(n+m)\) time, their overall algorithmic runtime is thereby worst-case optimal. The bulk of their analysis is dedicated to charging the algorithmic runtime and query time to the workings of their heap, and to handling the special bottleneck vertices. We note that for any input _k_, their solution can also report the first _k_ elements of the sorted order in optimal time.

## Contribution.

We consider the setting from \[5\], where the input is a directed acyclic graph _G_ over _X_ with _m_ edges and where, unlike \[3, 7, 11\], one does not separate the algorithmic performance between a pre-processing phase using _G_ and a phase that uses queries to _O<sub>L</sub>_. We show that this problem formulation allows for a surprisingly simple solution: _G_ denotes the input and _H<sub>i</sub>_ the graph at iteration _i_. Remove a maximum-length directed path \(\pi\) from _G_ to get _H_<sub>1</sub>. Iteratively<tbc>

<tbc>remove an _arbitrary_ source _x<sub>i</sub>_ from _H<sub>i</sub>_ to get _H_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. Insert _x<sub>i</sub>_ into \(\pi\) using _finger search_ where the finger _p<sub>i</sub>_ is the farthest in-neighbour of _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _G_ along \(\pi\) (we find _p<sub>i</sub>_ by simply iterating over all in-neighbours of _x<sub>i</sub>_). We use \(\Theta(n+m+loge(P_G))\) time and \(\Theta(loge(P_G))\) queries. We consider this algorithm to be simpler. Our proof of correctness is considerably simpler, as it relies upon only one counting argument and one geometric observation.

## 2 Algorithm

The input is a directed acyclic graph _G_ with vertex set _X_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_). This graph induces a partial order _P<sub>G</sub>_ where \(x_i\prec x_j\) if and only if there exists a directed path from _x<sub>i</sub>_ to _x<sub>j</sub>_ in _G_. The input also contains an oracle _O<sub>L</sub>_ that specifies a linear order _L_ over _X_. For any distinct _x<sub>i</sub>,x<sub>j</sub>_, an (oracle) query answers whether _x<sub>i</sub>\<<sub>L</sub>x<sub>j</sub>_. The goal is to output _X_ in its sorted order _L_.

We describe our algorithm. Our key observation is that the problem becomes significantly easier when we first extract a maximum-length directed path \(\pi\) from _G_. We iteratively remove an _arbitrary_ source _x<sub>i</sub>_ from \(H=G-\pi\) and insert it into \(\pi\). Once _H_ is empty, we return \(\pi\).

In our analysis, our logarithms are base 2 and _d_<sup>∗</sup>(_x<sub>i</sub>_) denotes the sum of the out-degree and the in-degree of a vertex _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _G_.

### Data structures.

We maintain a path \(\pi\) where for all vertices \(p,q\in\pi\): _p\<<sub>L</sub>q_ if and only if _p_ precedes _q_ in \(\pi\). We store the path \(\pi\) in a dynamic list order structure \(T_\pi\) which is a data structure that supports the following operations:

FingerInsert(_q<sub>i</sub>,x<sub>i</sub>_). Given vertices \(x_i\unknown\in\pi\) and \(q_i\in\pi\), insert _x<sub>i</sub>_ into \(\pi\) succeeding _q<sub>i</sub>_.

Search(_x<sub>i</sub>,p<sub>i</sub>,O<sub>L</sub>_). Given a vertex \(x_i\unknown\in\pi\) and a vertex \(p_i\in\pi\) with _p<sub>i</sub>\<<sub>L</sub>x<sub>i</sub>_. Return the farthest vertex _q<sub>i</sub>_ along \(\pi\) where _q<sub>i</sub>\<<sub>L</sub>x<sub>i</sub>_. Let _d<sub>i</sub>_ denote the number of vertices on the subpath from _p<sub>i</sub>_ to _q<sub>i</sub>_ along \(\pi\). We want to use _O_(1+log_d<sub>i</sub>_) time and queries to _O<sub>L</sub>_.

Compare(_p,q_). Given \(p,q\in\pi\), return _q_ if it succeeds _p_ in \(\pi\) in _O_(1) time (return _p_ otherwise). To achieve this, we store \(\pi\) in leaf-linked a balanced finger search tree \(T_\pi\). Many implementations exist \[2\]. We choose the level-linked (2-4)-tree by Huddleston and Mehlhorn \[6\], which supports FingerInsert in amortised _O_(1)-time, and Search in _O_(1+log_d<sub>i</sub>_) time. For Compare, we store the linked leaves in the simple dynamic list ordering structure by Bender et al. \[1\] whose simplest implementation supports Compare in _O_(1) time, and FingerInsert in amortised _O_(1) time.

### Algorithm and runtime analysis.

Our algorithm is straightforward. The pseudo code is given by Algorithm 1 where each algorithmic step also indicates the running time. We require linear space. We first extract a longest directed path \(\pi\) from _G_, which we store in our two data structures. This takes _O(n+m_) total time. If \(\pi\) has _n-k_ vertices, this leaves us with a graph _H_ with _k_ vertices.

We then iteratively remove an arbitrary source _x<sub>i</sub>_ from _H_. Since _x<sub>i</sub>_ is a source in _H_, all vertices \(p\in X\) that have a directed path to _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _G_ must be present in \(\pi\). We iterate over all in-neighbours of _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _G_, and use our Compare operation to find the in-neighbour _p<sub>i</sub>_ that is furthest along \(\pi\). If _x<sub>i</sub>_ has no in-neighbours, _p<sub>i</sub>_ is a dummy vertex that precedes the head of \(\pi\) instead. Finally, we proceed in a way that is very similar to the algorithm for topological sorting by Knuth \[10\]: We remove _x<sub>i</sub>_ from _H_, iterate over all out-neighbours of _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _H_ and decrement their in-degree, and update the linked list of sources to include the newly found ones. Since we inspect each in- and out-edge of _x<sub>i</sub>_ only once, this takes _O(m_) total time.

We then want to find the farthest _q<sub>i</sub>_ along \(\pi\) that precedes _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _L_. In the special case where _p<sub>i</sub>_ is the dummy vertex preceding the head _h_ of \(\pi\), we use a query to _O<sub>L</sub>_ to check whether _x<sub>i</sub>\<sub>L</sub>h_. If<tbc>

**Algorithm 1** Sort(directed acyclic graph _G_ over a ground set _X_, Oracle _O<sub>L</sub>_) time

1: \(\pi\leftarrow\) a longest directed path in _G_ \(\triangleright O(n+m)\)

2: \(T_\pi\leftarrow\) a level-linked (2-4)-tree over \(\pi\) \[6\] \(\triangleright O(n)\)

3: \(H\leftarrow G-\pi\) \(\triangleright O(n+m)\)

4: Compute for each vertex in _H_ its in-degree in _H_ \(\triangleright O(n+m)\)

5: \(S\leftarrow\) sources in _H_ \(\triangleright O(n)\)

6: **while** \(S\neq\emptyset\) **do**

7: Remove an arbitrary vertex _x<sub>i</sub>_ from _S_ \(\triangleright O(1)\)

8: \(p_i\leftarrow\) a dummy vertex, which is prepended before the head of \(\pi\) \(\triangleright O(1)\)

9: **for all** in-neighbors _u_ of _x<sub>i</sub>_ in _G_ **do** \(\triangleright O(d^*(x_i))\)

10: \(p_i\leftarrow\) Compare(_p<sub>i</sub>,u_) \(\triangleright O(1)\)

11: Remove _x<sub>i</sub>_ from _H_ and add any new sources in _H_ to _S_ \(\triangleright O(d^*(x_i))\)

12: \(q_i\leftarrow\) Search(_x<sub>i</sub>,p<sub>i</sub>,O<sub>L</sub>_) \(\triangleright O(1+logd_i)\)

13: FingerInsert(_q<sub>i</sub>,x<sub>i</sub>_) \(\triangleright O(1)\) amortised

14: **return** the leaves of \(T_\pi\) in order \(\triangleright O(n)\)

so, we return _q<sub>i</sub>=p<sub>i</sub>_. Otherwise, we set _p<sub>i</sub>=h_ and invoke Search. This returns _q<sub>i</sub>_ in _O_(1+log_d<sub>i</sub>_) time and queries, where _d<sub>i</sub>_ is the length of the subpath from _p<sub>i</sub>_ to _q<sub>i</sub>_ in \(\pi\) (_d<sub>i</sub>_=1 if _p<sub>i</sub>=q<sub>i</sub>_).

Finally, we insert _x<sub>i</sub>_ into \(T_\pi\) succeeding _q<sub>i</sub>_ in constant time. Updating the dynamic list order data structure and rebalancing \(T_\pi\) takes amortised _O_(1) time. Thus, these operations take _O(n_) total time over all insertions. Therefore, our algorithm uses \(O\big(n+m+\sum_{x_i\in H}(1+logd_i)\big)\) time and \(O\big(\sum_{x_i\in H}(1+logd_i)\big)\) queries.

## 2.1 Proof of optimality

Recall that _e(P<sub>G</sub>_) denotes the number of linear extensions of _P<sub>G</sub>_ and let _H_ start out with _k_ vertices. For ease of analysis, we re-index the vertices _X_ so that the path \(\pi\) are vertices (_x_<sub>_k_+1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_), in order, and _x<sub>i</sub>_ for \(i\in[k]\) is the _i_’th vertex our algorithm inserts into \(T_\pi\). We prove that our algorithm is tight by showing that \(\sum_{i=1}^k(1+logd_i)=k+\sum_{i=1}^klogd_i\in O(loge(P_G))\).

**Lemma 1.** _Let G be a directed acyclic graph, P<sub>G</sub> be its induced partial order and_ \(\pi\) _be a longest directed path in G. If_ \(\pi\) _has n-k vertices then_ \(loge(P_G)\ge k\).

_Proof._ Denote \(\ell(x)\) the length of the longest directed path in _G_ from a vertex _x_. Denote for \(i\in[n]\) by \(L_i:=|\{x\in X|\ell(x)=i\}|\). For each \(i\in[n-k]\), there is one \(u\in\pi\) with \(\ell(u)=i\) so:

\(k=\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}(L_i-1).\) (1)

Consider a linear order \(L'\) that is obtained by first sorting all \(x\in X\) by \(\ell(x)\) from high to low, and ordering (_u,v_) with \(\ell(u)=\ell(v)\) arbitrarily. The order \(L'\) must extend _P<sub>G</sub>_, since any vertex _w_ that has a directed path towards a vertex _u_ must have that \(\ell(w)>\ell(u)\). We count the number of distinct \(L'\) that we obtain in this way to lower bound _e(P<sub>G</sub>_):

\(e(P_G)\ge\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}L_i!\Rightarrow e(P_G)\ge\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}2^{L_i-1}=2\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}(L_i-1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{(L_i-1)}}\Rightarrow e(P_G)\ge 2^k\)

Here, the first implication uses that \(x!\ge 2^{x-1}\) and the second implication uses Equation 1.

What remains is to show that \(\sum_{i=1}^klogd_i\in O(loge(P_G))\). To this end, we create a set of intervals:

**Definition 1.** _Let_ \(\pi^*\) _be the directed path that Algorithm 1 outputs. For any_ \(i\in[n]\) _denote by_ \(\pi^*(x_i)\) _the index of x<sub>i</sub> in_ \(\pi^*\)_. We create an embedding E of X by placing x<sub>i</sub> at position_ \(\pi^*(x_i)\).

_Recall that for_ \(i\in[k]\)_, p<sub>i</sub> is the finger from where Algorithm 1 invokes_ Search _with x<sub>i</sub> as the argument. We create as set_ R _of n open intervals_ \(R_i=(a_i,b_i)\subseteq[0,n]\) _as follows:_

• _If i\>k then_ \((a_i,b_i):=(\pi^*(x_i)-1,\pi^*(x_i))\).<tbc>

• _Else,_ \((a_i,b_i):=(\pi^*(p_i),\pi^*(x_i))\).

**Lemma 2.** _Given distinct_ \(x_i,x_j\in X\)_. If there exists a directed path from x<sub>i</sub> to x<sub>j</sub> in G then the intervals R<sub>i</sub>_=(_a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>_) _and R<sub>j</sub>_=(_a<sub>j</sub>,b<sub>j</sub>_) _are disjoint with_ \(b_i\le a_j\).

_Proof._ We consider three cases.

If _i\>k_ and _j\>k_ then _x<sub>i</sub>_ and _x<sub>j</sub>_ are part of the original longest directed path in _G_. If _x<sub>i</sub>_ has a directed path to _x<sub>j</sub>_ in _G_ then _x<sub>i</sub>_ precedes _x<sub>j</sub>_ on the original longest directed path. Thus, \(\pi^*(x_i)\) precedes \(\pi^*(x_j)\) and _R<sub>i</sub>_ and _R<sub>j</sub>_ are distinct unit intervals where _R<sub>i</sub>_ precedes _R<sub>j</sub>_.

If \(i\le k\) and _j\>k_ then _x<sub>i</sub>_ was inserted into the path \(\pi\) with _x<sub>j</sub>_ already in \(\pi\). Since \(\pi^*\) is a linear extension of _P<sub>G</sub>_, it follows that _x<sub>i</sub>_ was inserted preceding _x<sub>j</sub>_ in \(\pi\). It follows that _x<sub>i</sub>_ precedes _x<sub>j</sub>_ in \(\pi^*\) and thus \(R_i=(\pi^*(p_i),\pi^*(x_i))\) lies strictly before \(R_j=(\pi^*(x_j)-1,\pi^*(x_j))\).

If \(j\le k\) then the vertex _p<sub>j</sub>_ must equal or succeed _x<sub>i</sub>_ in the path \(\pi^*\). It follows that \(b_i=\pi^*(x_i)\le a_i=\pi^*(p_j)\). The fact that these intervals are open then makes them disjoint.

The set R induces an interval order _P_<sub>R</sub> over _X_, which is the partial order \(\prec_\mathcal{R}\) where _x<sub>i</sub>_ and _x<sub>j</sub>_ are incomparable whenever _R<sub>i</sub>_ and _R<sub>j</sub>_ intersect, and where otherwise \(x_i\prec_\mathcal{R}x_j\) whenever \(b_i\le a_j\). By Lemma 2, any linear order _L_ that extends _P_<sub>R</sub> must also extend _P<sub>G</sub>_ and so \(e(P_\mathcal{R})\le e(P_G)\). The number of linear extensions of an interval order is much easier to count. In fact, Cardinal, Fiorini, Joret, Jungers and Munro \[3\] and Van der Hoog, Kostityna, Löffler and Speckmann \[11\] already upper bound the number of linear extensions of an interval order. We paraphrase their upper bound, to give a weaker version applicable to this paper. For a proof from first principles, see Section 3.

**Lemma 3** (Lemma 1 in \[11\] and Lemma 3.2 in \[3\])**.** _Let_ R=(_R_<sub>1</sub>_,...R<sub>n</sub>_) _be a set of n open intervals in_ \[0_,n_\] _and let each interval have at least unit size. Let P_<sub>R</sub> _be its induced partial order. Then:_

\(\sum_{i=1}^nlog(|R_i|)\in O(loge(P_\mathcal{R})).\)

We are now ready to prove our main theorem:

**Theorem 1.** _Given a directed acyclic graph G over X, inducing a partial order P<sub>G</sub>, and an oracle O<sub>L</sub> whose queries specify a linear order L that extends P<sub>G</sub>, there exists an algorithm that uses linear space, O(n+m_+log_e(P<sub>G</sub>_)) _time and O_(log_e(P<sub>G</sub>_)) _oracle queries to output the sorted order of X._

_Proof._ Our algorithm runs in \(O(n+m+k+\sum_{i=1}^klogd_i)\) time and uses \(O(k+\sum_{i=1}^klogd_i)\) queries. By Lemma 1, \(k\in O(loge(P_G))\). The set R of Definition 1 is a set where each interval _R<sub>i</sub>_ has at least unit size. By Lemma 2, \(e(P_\mathcal{R})\le e(P_G)\). For \(i\le k\), the size |_R<sub>i</sub>_| must be at least _d<sub>i</sub>_ since there are per construction at least _d<sub>i</sub>_ vertices on the subpath from \(\pi^*(p_i)\) to \(\pi^*(q_j)\) in the embedding _E_. It follows by Lemma 3 that \(\sum_{i=1}^klogd_i\in O(loge(P_\mathcal{R}))\subseteq O(loge(P_G))\).

## 3 Deriving Lemma 3 from first principles

We consider the following statement:

**Lemma 3** (Lemma 1 in \[11\] and Lemma 3.2 in \[3\])**.** _Let_ R=(_R_<sub>1</sub>_,...R<sub>n</sub>_) _be a set of n open intervals in_ \[0_,n_\] _and let each interval have at least unit size. Let P_<sub>R</sub> _be its induced partial order. Then:_<tbc>

\(\sum_{i=1}^nlog(|R_i|)\in O(loge(P_\mathcal{R})).\)

<tbc>While this lemma follows verbatim from Lemma 1 in \[11\] (which itself is weaker version of Lemma 3.2 in in \[3\]), we also give a proof from first principles. We reindex R so that (_R_<sub>1</sub>_,R_<sub>2</sub>_,...,R<sub>m</sub>_) is a maximum cardinality set of pairwise-disjoint intervals in _R_, sorted from left to right. For any \(R_i\in\mathcal{R}\) we denote by mid(_R<sub>i</sub>_) its centre. We define an (_n-m_)-dimensional polytope associated with R.

\(A=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\big|x_i=mid(R_i)\text{for}i\le m\text{and}x_i\in R_i\text{for}i>m\right\}\)

The volume of this polytope is \(Vol(A)=\prod_{i=m+1}^n|R_i|\). Any \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in A\) with distinct coordinates defines a linear extension _L_ of _P_<sub>R</sub> via the rule "\(i\prec j\) if and only if _x<sub>i</sub>\<x<sub>j</sub>_". We call the point _x_ a _realisation of L_. Observe that not all linear extensions of _P_<sub>R</sub> have a realisation \(x\in A\).

**Claim 1.** _Let L be a linear extension of P<sub>R</sub>. Let_ \(A_L=\left\{x\in A\big|x\text{realises}L\right\}\)_, then_<tbc>

\(Vol(A_L)\le(2e)^{n-m}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Consider the _m_+1 open intervals:<tbc>

\(I:=(-0.5,mid(R_1)),\dots,(mid(R_i),mid(R_{i+1})),\dots,(mid(R_{m-1}),n+0.5).\)

<tbc>For all \((i,j)\in[m]\times[m]\), the intervals (_R<sub>i</sub>,R<sub>j</sub>_) are disjoint and have length at least 1. It follows that each interval in _I_ has length at least 1. Suppose that _L_ cannot be realised, then Vol(_A<sub>L</sub>_)=0. Otherwise, we observe that for any \(x,x'\) realising _L_ and any \(i\in\{m+1,\dots,n\}\), an interval in _I_ contains _x<sub>i</sub>_ if and only if it contains \(x'_i\). This allows us to say that an interval in _I_ is _occupied under L_ if it contains _x<sub>i</sub>_ for any realisation _x_ of _L_ and any _i\>m_. There are at most _n-m_ occupied intervals, and therefore at least _m_+1-(_n-m_)=(2_m_+1-_n_) non-occupied intervals in _I_. Let _G<sub>L</sub>_ be the union of the occupied intervals. Then \(|G_L|\le|(-0.5,n+0.5)|-(2m+1-n)=2(n-m)\), as each non-occupied interval has length at least 1. Let:<tbc>

\(B_L=\left\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m\times G_L^{n-m}\big|y_i=mid(R_i)\text{for}i\le m\text{and}(x_j<x_k\Leftrightarrow y_j<y_k)\text{for}j,k>m\right\}.\)
